question: A 72-year-old man develops progressive shortness of breath one week after an episode of chest pain. He is orthopneic, uses three pillows at night, has jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles, pink frothy sputum, and a chest radiograph showing cardiomegaly with bilateral perihilar airspace opacities. Which of the following best explains the primary mechanism producing his pulmonary findings?
cited_learning_objective: Compare pathophysiological manifestations of cardiogenic and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema

options.text: Elevated pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure from impaired left ventricular function
options.rationale: Correct because cardiogenic pulmonary edema results from left ventricular failure raising pulmonary venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure, forcing fluid into interstitium and alveoli as described in the lecture.

options.text: Increased alveolar capillary permeability due to diffuse inflammatory injury
options.rationale: Wrong because increased permeability is the mechanism of noncardiogenic edema (eg, ARDS); this would be correct only if the patient had sepsis, inhalational injury, or direct lung insult rather than left heart dysfunction.

options.text: Marked reduction in plasma oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia
options.rationale: Wrong because decreased plasma oncotic pressure causes edema when hypoalbuminemia is present; it would be correct only if laboratory data showed low serum albumin and no cardiac enlargement.

options.text: Obstruction of pulmonary lymphatic drainage causing interstitial fluid accumulation
options.rationale: Wrong because lymphatic obstruction produces interstitial edema over time (eg, lymphangitic carcinomatosis); it would be correct only if imaging and history suggested lymphatic blockage rather than acute LV failure.

options.text: Rapid decrease in interstitial pressure after thoracentesis causing fluid shift into alveoli
options.rationale: Wrong because decreased interstitial pressure causing edema is seen after rapid removal of pleural fluid; it would be correct only if the patient had recent large-volume pleural drainage preceding symptoms.

question: Which of the following clinical features from the lecture most specifically distinguishes cardiogenic pulmonary edema from noncardiogenic pulmonary edema in a patient with acute hypoxemia?
cited_learning_objective: Compare pathophysiological manifestations of cardiogenic and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema

options.text: Elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure on right heart catheterization
options.rationale: Correct because cardiogenic (hydrostatic) edema is associated with increased PAWP reflecting left atrial pressure; the lecture states PAWP is high in cardiogenic edema and normal or low in noncardiogenic causes.

options.text: Severe hypoxemia with normal cardiac size on chest radiograph
options.rationale: Wrong because severe hypoxemia and normal heart size are typical of noncardiogenic edema; this would be correct only if imaging showed no cardiomegaly and PAWP was normal.

options.text: Presence of Kerley B lines on chest radiograph
options.rationale: Wrong because Kerley B lines indicate interstitial fluid and are more characteristic of cardiogenic edema but are not specific; this option would be correct only if correlated with elevated PAWP and cardiomegaly.

options.text: Requirement for diuretics as first-line therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because diuretics are first-line for cardiogenic edema but this is a management choice rather than a distinguishing diagnostic feature; it would be correct only in the context of confirmed cardiogenic physiology.

options.text: Diffuse bilateral infiltrates with no cardiomegaly on chest radiograph
options.rationale: Wrong because this pattern suggests noncardiogenic edema; it would be correct only if PAWP were normal and there was an inflammatory or direct lung injury cause.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary edema has an arterial blood gas showing PaO₂ 55 mmHg, PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, and pH 7.49. Based on the lecture, what best explains the low PaCO₂ in early cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the respiratory manifestations of pulmonary edema

options.text: Hyperventilation of functioning alveoli causing respiratory alkalosis
options.rationale: Correct because early pulmonary edema causes hypoxemia that stimulates hyperventilation of remaining functional alveoli, lowering PaCO₂ and producing alkalosis as described in the lecture.

options.text: Impaired CO₂ diffusion across flooded alveoli causing hypocapnia
options.rationale: Wrong because impaired diffusion would raise PaCO₂; this would be correct only if CO₂ elimination were reduced rather than increased by hyperventilation.

options.text: Increased metabolic production of CO₂ with renal compensation
options.rationale: Wrong because increased CO₂ production would raise PaCO₂; this option would be correct only if metabolic rate were markedly elevated and ventilation inadequate.

options.text: Primary respiratory muscle weakness reducing CO₂ retention
options.rationale: Wrong because respiratory muscle weakness causes hypoventilation and CO₂ retention; it would be correct only if the patient had neuromuscular disease causing hypoventilation.

options.text: Alveolar hyperperfusion increasing CO₂ washout
options.rationale: Wrong because alveolar hyperperfusion is not the mechanism; the correct mechanism is increased ventilation of functional units, not increased perfusion.

question: A 57-year-old postoperative patient develops sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, and hypoxemia on postoperative day 4. Examination shows unilateral calf swelling and tenderness. According to the lecture, from which venous sites do most clinically significant pulmonary emboli originate?
cited_learning_objective: Classify the risk factors for pulmonary embolism

options.text: Deep veins of the lower extremity such as femoral and popliteal veins
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states that 95% of pulmonary emboli arise from deep venous thromboses in the leg (tibial, popliteal, femoral).

options.text: Pulmonary veins draining the lung parenchyma
options.rationale: Wrong because pulmonary emboli originate from systemic venous thrombi, not pulmonary veins; this would be correct only if a paradoxical embolus passed through a right-to-left shunt into arterial circulation.

options.text: Upper extremity superficial veins after peripheral IV placement
options.rationale: Wrong because superficial upper extremity clots rarely cause major PE; this would be correct only if a large deep venous thrombosis of the upper limb were present.

options.text: Portal venous system from abdominal sources
options.rationale: Wrong because portal venous thrombi do not embolize to pulmonary arteries unless there is an abnormal shunt; it would be correct only with a portosystemic vascular anomaly.

options.text: Left atrial appendage thrombus from atrial fibrillation
options.rationale: Wrong because left atrial thrombi embolize to systemic arterial circulation, not pulmonary arteries; this would be correct only if there were an intracardiac shunt allowing paradoxical embolization.

question: Which combination of Virchow’s triad elements listed in the lecture best explains the high risk of venous thromboembolism after major orthopedic surgery?
cited_learning_objective: Classify the risk factors for pulmonary embolism

options.text: Venous stasis from immobility and endothelial injury from surgery
options.rationale: Correct because postoperative patients have prolonged immobility (venous stasis) and surgical manipulation causes endothelial injury, both components of Virchow's triad emphasized in the lecture.

options.text: Hyperviscosity from polycythemia and systemic infection
options.rationale: Wrong because while hyperviscosity and inflammation can contribute, the classic postoperative risk is stasis and endothelial injury; this option would be correct only if lab evidence of polycythemia and infection were present.

options.text: Arterial hypertension and atherosclerotic plaque rupture
options.rationale: Wrong because arterial hypertension and plaque rupture cause arterial thrombosis, not venous thromboembolism; it would be correct only in an arterial thrombotic context.

options.text: Hypoalbuminemia causing decreased plasma oncotic pressure
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoalbuminemia predisposes to edema, not venous thrombosis; this would be correct only if the question asked about edema rather than thromboembolism.

options.text: Pulmonary vasoconstriction from hypoxia and chronic lung disease
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoxic vasoconstriction contributes to pulmonary hypertension, not initial venous thrombus formation; it would be correct only if chronic hypoxia were the primary pathology.

question: A patient with a large central pulmonary arterial occlusion develops hypotension and signs of right ventricular strain. Based on the lecture, which immediate hemodynamic consequence most directly reduces left ventricular preload?
cited_learning_objective: Understand clinical manifestations of pulmonary embolism

options.text: Acute right ventricular dilation decreasing left ventricular filling
options.rationale: Correct because central PE causes RV overload and distension, which shifts the interventricular septum and reduces LV preload, leading to hypotension as described in the lecture.

options.text: Systemic vasodilation from inflammatory mediators lowering venous return
options.rationale: Wrong because systemic vasodilation is not the primary immediate effect of acute PE; this would be correct only if a distributive shock process were concurrently present.

options.text: Increased left atrial pressure causing pulmonary venous congestion
options.rationale: Wrong because increased left atrial pressure is characteristic of left heart failure, not acute PE; it would be correct only if left-sided cardiac dysfunction were the cause.

options.text: Loss of pulmonary surfactant leading to alveolar collapse and reduced venous return
options.rationale: Wrong because surfactant loss causes alveolar collapse and hypoxemia but does not directly reduce LV preload; it would be correct only in severe ARDS with secondary hemodynamic effects.

options.text: Massive pulmonary hemorrhage decreasing circulating blood volume
options.rationale: Wrong because pulmonary hemorrhage is not the typical immediate consequence of PE; this would be correct only if there were concurrent major intrapulmonary bleeding causing hypovolemia.

question: A patient suspected of pulmonary embolism has an early arterial blood gas showing low PaO₂ and low PaCO₂ with elevated pH. According to the lecture, which ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) change primarily explains the initial hypoxemia?
cited_learning_objective: Understand clinical manifestations of pulmonary embolism

options.text: Increased physiologic dead space in embolized regions with redistribution causing low V/Q elsewhere
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that embolized regions become dead space (high V/Q) and blood redistribution to remaining units lowers V/Q there, producing hypoxemia and hyperventilation.

options.text: Global diffusion impairment across all alveolar membranes
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion impairment is not the primary mechanism in acute PE; it would be correct only with interstitial lung disease or thickened alveolar-capillary membranes.

options.text: Uniform shunting of blood through nonventilated alveoli
options.rationale: Wrong because PE causes increased dead space rather than uniform shunt; this option would be correct only if large areas of alveoli were filled with fluid or collapsed.

options.text: Decreased ventilation to perfused units due to bronchospasm
options.rationale: Wrong because bronchospasm is not the main driver in PE-related hypoxemia; it would be correct only if the patient had concurrent severe reactive airway disease.

options.text: Increased intrapulmonary shunt from pulmonary capillary leak
options.rationale: Wrong because capillary leak causing shunt is characteristic of ARDS or noncardiogenic edema, not the initial physiology of acute PE; it would be correct only with inflammatory lung injury.

question: Which diagnostic test does the lecture identify as the first-choice imaging modality to demonstrate a pulmonary arterial filling defect in a hemodynamically stable patient suspected of pulmonary embolism?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the diagnostic options for pulmonary embolism

options.text: Computed tomography pulmonary angiography demonstrating intraluminal filling defect
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states CTPA is the first-choice test to visualize filling defects in pulmonary arteries, except when contraindicated by renal failure or contrast allergy.

options.text: Ventilation perfusion scan showing matched perfusion defects
options.rationale: Wrong because V/Q scanning is reserved when CTPA is contraindicated; it would be correct only if the patient had renal insufficiency or contrast allergy preventing CTPA.

options.text: Chest radiograph showing Hampton's hump as definitive evidence
options.rationale: Wrong because chest x-ray findings like Hampton's hump are neither sensitive nor specific; this would be correct only if combined with other definitive imaging.

options.text: Pulmonary angiography via catheter as the routine first-line test
options.rationale: Wrong because invasive pulmonary angiography is not first-line; it would be correct only if noninvasive imaging were inconclusive and intervention was planned.

options.text: Lower extremity venous duplex ultrasound as the definitive test for PE
options.rationale: Wrong because venous duplex can detect DVT but does not directly visualize pulmonary emboli; it would be correct only if a proximal DVT were found and imaging contraindicated.

question: A patient with multiple long-bone fractures becomes acutely confused and hypoxemic 48 hours after injury and develops a petechial rash on the chest. Based on the lecture, which pathophysiologic process best accounts for the pulmonary component of this syndrome?
cited_learning_objective: Characterize the pathophysiological and clinical manifestations of fat embolism syndrome

options.text: Mechanical obstruction of pulmonary capillaries by marrow fat globules with secondary inflammation
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture describes fat embolism as fat globules lodging in pulmonary capillaries causing mechanical obstruction and later inflammatory injury leading to ARDS-like pulmonary edema.

options.text: Thromboembolism from deep leg veins causing large central arterial occlusion
options.rationale: Wrong because thromboembolism is a different entity (PE); this would be correct only if imaging showed a thrombus rather than fat globules and there was DVT evidence.

options.text: Aspiration of gastric contents causing chemical pneumonitis
options.rationale: Wrong because aspiration causes direct alveolar injury and inflammation but not the triad of neurologic signs and petechiae seen in fat embolism; it would be correct only with witnessed aspiration.

options.text: Septic emboli from infected bone fragments causing multifocal pneumonia
options.rationale: Wrong because septic emboli produce infectious foci and fever; this would be correct only if cultures and imaging supported septic embolization.

options.text: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from blood transfusion reactions
options.rationale: Wrong because transfusion reactions cause TRALI and not the classic neurologic and petechial triad; it would be correct only with recent transfusion and compatible serology.

question: Which triad of clinical findings from the lecture is most characteristic of fat embolism syndrome?
cited_learning_objective: Characterize the pathophysiological and clinical manifestations of fat embolism syndrome

options.text: Hypoxemia, neurologic abnormalities, and petechial rash
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture defines the clinical triad of fat embolism syndrome as lung (hypoxemia), brain (neurologic signs), and skin (petechial rash).

options.text: Fever, productive cough, and lobar consolidation on chest x-ray
options.rationale: Wrong because these findings suggest pneumonia rather than fat embolism; it would be correct only with infectious evidence and positive cultures.

options.text: Hemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, and calf swelling
options.rationale: Wrong because this constellation is more typical of pulmonary thromboembolism with infarction; it would be correct only if DVT and imaging confirmed PE.

options.text: Wheezing, eosinophilia, and peripheral eosinophilic infiltrates
options.rationale: Wrong because these features indicate allergic or eosinophilic lung disease; it would be correct only with supporting lab and biopsy findings.

options.text: Acute onset hematuria, flank pain, and oliguria
options.rationale: Wrong because these are renal symptoms not characteristic of fat embolism; it would be correct only if renal embolization or injury were primary.

question: A patient with suspected fat embolism syndrome has thrombocytopenia and signs of microthrombi formation. According to the lecture, what hematologic mechanism explains these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Characterize the pathophysiological and clinical manifestations of fat embolism syndrome

options.text: Platelet aggregation around fat globules causing microthrombi and consumption
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes that platelets and fibrin activate around fat globules, forming microthrombi that can lead to thrombocytopenia and DIC-like states.

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of platelets mediated by antiplatelet antibodies
options.rationale: Wrong because immune thrombocytopenia is not the mechanism in FES; it would be correct only with positive antiplatelet antibody testing and chronic presentation.

options.text: Bone marrow suppression causing decreased platelet production
options.rationale: Wrong because marrow suppression reduces production over days to weeks, not the acute platelet consumption seen in FES; it would be correct only with marrow biopsy evidence.

options.text: Hemodilution from aggressive crystalloid resuscitation lowering platelet concentration
options.rationale: Wrong because hemodilution is a dilutional effect rather than platelet activation and microthrombi formation; it would be correct only if large-volume resuscitation preceded labs.

options.text: Sequestration of platelets in an enlarged spleen causing thrombocytopenia
options.rationale: Wrong because splenic sequestration is a chronic process and not the acute consumptive coagulopathy described in FES; it would be correct only with splenomegaly on exam or imaging.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary edema shows a chest x-ray with bilateral perihilar 'bat-wing' opacities, cardiomegaly, and Kerley B lines. Which of the following treatments listed in the lecture is most appropriate as an immediate intervention for cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the diagnostic options for pulmonary embolism

options.text: Loop diuretic administration and upright positioning with supplemental oxygen
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture recommends diuretics (eg, furosemide), sitting the patient upright, and oxygen as initial management for cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

options.text: High positive end-expiratory pressure ventilation without diuretics
options.rationale: Wrong because PEEP and mechanical ventilation are first-line for noncardiogenic edema (eg, ARDS); this would be correct only if the edema were noncardiogenic and refractory to oxygen.

options.text: Immediate corticosteroids to reduce capillary permeability
options.rationale: Wrong because corticosteroids are not standard acute therapy for cardiogenic edema; they are considered in inflammatory causes like FES and would be correct only with inflammatory etiology.

options.text: Aggressive crystalloid bolus to improve preload and cardiac output
options.rationale: Wrong because fluid bolus worsens hydrostatic pulmonary edema from LV failure; it would be correct only if the patient were hypovolemic with low filling pressures.

options.text: Immediate anticoagulation with heparin as primary therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because anticoagulation treats thromboembolism, not cardiogenic pulmonary edema; it would be correct only if PE were the confirmed cause of hypoxemia.

question: A patient with sepsis develops diffuse bilateral infiltrates and severe hypoxemia with normal cardiac size and normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. According to the lecture, which category best classifies this pulmonary edema?
cited_learning_objective: Compare pathophysiological manifestations of cardiogenic and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema

options.text: Permeability pulmonary edema due to increased capillary leak (noncardiogenic)
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture describes noncardiogenic edema (eg, ARDS) as permeability-related from inflammation with normal PCWP and usually no cardiomegaly.

options.text: Hydrostatic pulmonary edema from left ventricular failure
options.rationale: Wrong because hydrostatic (cardiogenic) edema shows cardiomegaly and elevated PCWP; it would be correct only if LV dysfunction and elevated wedge pressure were present.

options.text: Edema from decreased plasma oncotic pressure due to hypoalbuminemia
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoalbuminemia causes generalized edema and low oncotic pressure; it would be correct only if serum albumin were markedly reduced and cardiac function normal.

options.text: Interstitial edema from lymphatic obstruction by malignancy
options.rationale: Wrong because lymphatic obstruction causes chronic interstitial edema; it would be correct only with imaging or history of lymphangitic carcinomatosis.

options.text: Edema from rapid removal of pleural fluid lowering interstitial pressure
options.rationale: Wrong because decreased interstitial pressure after thoracentesis can cause edema; it would be correct only if there were recent large-volume pleural drainage.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary embolism has a V/Q scan showing large perfusion defects with preserved ventilation in the same regions. Based on the lecture, how does this pattern affect the physiologic V/Q ratio in the affected lung units?
cited_learning_objective: Understand clinical manifestations of pulmonary embolism

options.text: V/Q ratio approaches infinity due to absent perfusion with preserved ventilation
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that complete obstruction of a pulmonary artery produces regions with ventilation but no perfusion, increasing V/Q toward infinity (dead space).

options.text: V/Q ratio approaches zero due to absent ventilation with preserved perfusion
options.rationale: Wrong because V/Q near zero describes shunt physiology where ventilation is absent; it would be correct only if alveoli were filled with fluid or collapsed.

options.text: V/Q ratio equals 1.0 indicating perfect matching
options.rationale: Wrong because perfect matching is not seen with large perfusion defects; it would be correct only in healthy lung units with matched ventilation and perfusion.

options.text: V/Q ratio decreases to 0.5 due to mild perfusion reduction
options.rationale: Wrong because a complete perfusion defect causes a much larger change than a mild reduction; this would be correct only with partial perfusion loss.

options.text: V/Q ratio becomes 0.8 reflecting slight mismatch
options.rationale: Wrong because 0.8 is near-normal and does not represent the dead-space physiology of PE; it would be correct only with minimal V/Q disturbance.

question: A 46-year-old postoperative patient develops sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. ABG shows pH 7.53 [7.35-7.45], PaO₂ 65 mmHg [80-100], PaCO₂ 28 mmHg [35-45], HCO₃⁻ 23 mEq/L [22-26]. According to the lecture, which acid-base disturbance best matches these values and the typical early response to pulmonary embolism?
cited_learning_objective: Understand clinical manifestations of pulmonary embolism

options.text: Acute respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation due to hypoxemia
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes that early PE causes hypoxemia leading to hyperventilation, low PaCO₂, and respiratory alkalosis with elevated pH.

options.text: Metabolic alkalosis from diuretic overuse causing low PaCO₂
options.rationale: Wrong because metabolic alkalosis would show elevated HCO₃⁻; this would be correct only if HCO₃⁻ were increased due to diuretics or vomiting.

options.text: Acute respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation causing hypercapnia
options.rationale: Wrong because respiratory acidosis shows elevated PaCO₂ and low pH; it would be correct only in late or failing respiratory compensation.

options.text: Mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis with low HCO₃⁻
options.rationale: Wrong because HCO₃⁻ is normal here; this mixed disorder would be correct only if HCO₃⁻ were decreased indicating metabolic acidosis.

options.text: Primary metabolic acidosis from lactic acid accumulation
options.rationale: Wrong because primary metabolic acidosis would lower pH and HCO₃⁻; it would be correct only if there were evidence of tissue hypoperfusion and low bicarbonate.

question: Which laboratory test mentioned in the lecture is most useful to exclude pulmonary embolism when it is negative in a low-risk patient?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the diagnostic options for pulmonary embolism

options.text: D-dimer assay with low pretest probability
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states that a negative D-dimer effectively excludes PE in patients with low clinical probability due to its high sensitivity.

options.text: Elevated cardiac troponin confirming pulmonary embolism
options.rationale: Wrong because troponin indicates RV strain or myocardial injury but is not sensitive enough to exclude PE; it would be correct only if elevated in the appropriate clinical context.

options.text: Arterial blood gas showing normal PaO₂ excluding PE
options.rationale: Wrong because ABG is neither sensitive nor specific for PE; normal PaO₂ does not exclude embolism and would be correct only with other negative testing.

options.text: Chest radiograph showing Hampton's hump confirming PE
options.rationale: Wrong because chest x-ray signs are neither sensitive nor specific; this would be correct only if combined with definitive imaging like CTPA.

options.text: Elevated BNP excluding PE in low-risk patients
options.rationale: Wrong because BNP reflects cardiac strain and is not used to exclude PE; it would be correct only if BNP were normal and other tests supported absence of RV strain.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary embolism is hemodynamically stable. According to the lecture, which is the primary long-term prevention strategy recommended for patients at risk of venous thromboembolism after major surgery?
cited_learning_objective: Classify the risk factors for pulmonary embolism

options.text: Pharmacologic anticoagulation prophylaxis during the postoperative period
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture emphasizes anticoagulant prophylaxis for postoperative patients to prevent venous thromboembolism, alongside mechanical measures like SCDs.

options.text: Routine placement of inferior vena cava filters in all postoperative patients
options.rationale: Wrong because IVC filters are reserved for selected cases with contraindications to anticoagulation; routine placement is not recommended and would be correct only with specific indications.

options.text: High-dose aspirin monotherapy for venous thrombosis prevention
options.rationale: Wrong because aspirin is not the standard prophylactic agent for postoperative VTE; it would be correct only in certain orthopedic protocols where aspirin is specifically indicated.

options.text: Prophylactic systemic thrombolysis immediately after surgery
options.rationale: Wrong because thrombolytics carry high bleeding risk and are not used prophylactically; it would be correct only in life-threatening thrombosis where benefits outweigh bleeding risk.

options.text: Extended bed rest to minimize movement and clot propagation
options.rationale: Wrong because immobility increases venous stasis and VTE risk; early ambulation and prophylaxis are recommended instead.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary embolism has an EKG showing S1Q3T3 pattern and elevated BNP. According to the lecture, what does an elevated BNP indicate in this context?
cited_learning_objective: Understand clinical manifestations of pulmonary embolism

options.text: Right ventricular strain or myocardial stretch from increased pulmonary vascular resistance
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes that elevated BNP in PE reflects RV overload and myocardial stretch due to increased pulmonary pressures.

options.text: Left ventricular systolic dysfunction causing pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Wrong because BNP can be elevated in LV failure but in PE the elevation specifically indicates RV strain; it would be correct only if LV dysfunction were documented.

options.text: Renal failure causing decreased BNP clearance
options.rationale: Wrong because renal impairment can raise BNP but in the acute PE setting BNP elevation is interpreted as cardiac strain; it would be correct only with concurrent renal dysfunction.

options.text: Primary pulmonary parenchymal inflammation raising BNP
options.rationale: Wrong because parenchymal inflammation does not directly elevate BNP; it would be correct only if inflammation caused significant cardiac strain.

options.text: Chronic liver disease causing altered peptide metabolism
options.rationale: Wrong because liver disease affects many proteins but is not the primary cause of acute BNP elevation in PE; it would be correct only with documented chronic hepatic dysfunction.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary embolism is found to have a large central clot causing RV overload and systemic hypotension. According to the lecture, which therapy is indicated for massive pulmonary embolism with hemodynamic compromise?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the diagnostic options for pulmonary embolism

options.text: Systemic thrombolytic therapy to rapidly dissolve obstructing thrombus
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists thrombolytics for massive PE with hemodynamic instability to rapidly reduce pulmonary vascular obstruction and RV afterload.

options.text: Routine long-term oral anticoagulation without acute reperfusion
options.rationale: Wrong because anticoagulation alone may be insufficient in massive PE with shock; it would be correct only for submassive or low-risk PE without hemodynamic compromise.

options.text: Immediate high-volume crystalloid infusion as sole therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because fluids alone do not remove obstruction and may worsen RV dilation; it would be correct only as a temporizing measure in hypovolemia.

options.text: Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed septic emboli
options.rationale: Wrong because septic emboli are infectious and require antibiotics, but typical PE from DVT requires anticoagulation/thrombolysis; this would be correct only with evidence of infection.

options.text: Immediate placement of an inferior vena cava filter as first-line therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because IVC filters are reserved for contraindications to anticoagulation or recurrent PE despite therapy; they are not first-line for massive PE requiring reperfusion.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary edema demonstrates rapid shallow breathing and increased airway resistance on pulmonary function testing. According to the lecture, which mechanism best explains the reduced lung compliance in pulmonary edema?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the respiratory manifestations of pulmonary edema

options.text: Dilution and deactivation of surfactant increasing surface tension and reducing compliance
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that alveolar flooding dilutes surfactant, increases surface tension, causes alveolar collapse, and reduces lung compliance producing a restrictive pattern.

options.text: Bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy decreasing airway caliber
options.rationale: Wrong because bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy is a chronic change in asthma/COPD, not acute pulmonary edema; it would be correct only with chronic obstructive disease.

options.text: Loss of elastic fibers from emphysematous destruction increasing compliance
options.rationale: Wrong because emphysema increases compliance rather than decreasing it; this would be correct only in emphysematous disease, not edema.

options.text: Airway mucus plugging causing fixed airflow obstruction
options.rationale: Wrong because mucus plugging causes obstructive physiology rather than the restrictive pattern from decreased compliance; it would be correct only if mucus plugging were the dominant process.

options.text: Alveolar overdistension from excessive positive pressure ventilation
options.rationale: Wrong because overdistension increases compliance locally and is not the mechanism in pulmonary edema; it would be correct only in ventilator-induced lung injury with overinflation.

question: Which chest x-ray feature described in the lecture is most characteristic of interstitial pulmonary edema due to elevated hydrostatic pressure?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the respiratory manifestations of pulmonary edema

options.text: Kerley B lines representing thickened interlobular septa
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture identifies Kerley B lines as thickened interlobular septa from interstitial fluid accumulation typical of hydrostatic pulmonary edema.

options.text: Unilateral lobar consolidation indicating bacterial pneumonia
options.rationale: Wrong because lobar consolidation suggests pneumonia rather than interstitial edema; it would be correct only with infectious signs and focal consolidation.

options.text: Hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms indicating emphysema
options.rationale: Wrong because hyperinflation is seen in obstructive lung disease, not interstitial edema; it would be correct only with COPD physiology.

options.text: Miliary nodules diffusely scattered indicating hematogenous spread
options.rationale: Wrong because miliary nodules suggest disseminated infection or malignancy; it would be correct only with appropriate clinical context and imaging.

options.text: Localized pleural-based airspace opacity indicating pulmonary infarct
options.rationale: Wrong because a pleural-based opacity (Hampton's hump) can suggest infarct from PE but is not the classic interstitial Kerley B pattern of hydrostatic edema; it would be correct only with PE evidence.

question: A patient with acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema is noted to cough up frothy pink sputum. According to the lecture, what pathophysiologic process most directly produces the pink color in the sputum?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the respiratory manifestations of pulmonary edema

options.text: High capillary hydrostatic pressure causing red blood cell leakage into alveolar fluid
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that elevated capillary pressure can cause RBCs to leak into alveolar fluid, producing pink frothy sputum in cardiogenic edema.

options.text: Bacterial hemolysin producing hemoptysis in pneumonia
options.rationale: Wrong because bacterial hemolysins are not the typical cause of pink frothy sputum in pulmonary edema; this would be correct only with severe necrotizing infection.

options.text: Pulmonary embolus causing pulmonary infarction with frank hemorrhage
options.rationale: Wrong because PE-related infarction can cause hemoptysis but usually not the diffuse pink froth of edema; it would be correct only with peripheral infarction and bleeding.

options.text: Alveolar hemorrhage from vasculitis causing diffuse bloody sputum
options.rationale: Wrong because vasculitic alveolar hemorrhage produces frank blood rather than frothy pink sputum; it would be correct only with vasculitis evidence and hemoptysis.

options.text: Pulmonary edema fluid mixing with bile-stained secretions from aspiration
options.rationale: Wrong because aspiration yields foul or bilious sputum, not pink frothy sputum; it would be correct only with witnessed aspiration and appropriate contents.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary edema has an early arterial blood gas showing low PaO₂ and low PaCO₂. Later, the patient becomes fatigued and PaCO₂ rises with falling pH. According to the lecture, what does the late rise in PaCO₂ indicate?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the respiratory manifestations of pulmonary edema

options.text: Respiratory muscle fatigue and impending respiratory failure
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states that late in severe pulmonary edema PaCO₂ rises and pH falls, indicating respiratory failure from fatigue and inadequate ventilation.

options.text: Improved ventilation-perfusion matching resolving hyperventilation
options.rationale: Wrong because improved V/Q would normalize PaCO₂, not cause a rise with acidosis; it would be correct only if ventilation improved and CO₂ retention resolved.

options.text: Metabolic acidosis from renal failure causing compensatory hypoventilation
options.rationale: Wrong because metabolic acidosis typically causes hyperventilation to lower PaCO₂; this option would be correct only with primary metabolic disturbance and hypoventilation.

options.text: Excessive sedation causing central respiratory depression
options.rationale: Wrong because sedation can raise PaCO₂, but the lecture emphasizes fatigue and failure in late pulmonary edema; it would be correct only with documented sedative administration.

options.text: Bronchospasm causing airflow limitation and CO₂ retention
options.rationale: Wrong because bronchospasm causes obstructive physiology and CO₂ retention, but in pulmonary edema the primary late mechanism is ventilatory failure; it would be correct only with coexisting severe bronchospasm.

question: Which of the following mechanisms listed in the lecture is the primary driver of pulmonary arterial hypertension (Group 1) at the level of small pulmonary arteries?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the pathophysiology of pulmonary hypertension

options.text: Endothelial dysfunction with increased endothelin and decreased nitric oxide and prostacyclin
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture describes PAH as resulting from endothelial dysfunction with elevated endothelin-1 and reduced NO and PGI2, leading to vasoconstriction and remodeling.

options.text: Left atrial hypertension causing passive pulmonary venous congestion
options.rationale: Wrong because left atrial hypertension causes Group 2 postcapillary PH, not primary PAH; it would be correct only if wedge pressure were elevated.

options.text: Hypoxic vasoconstriction from chronic alveolar hypoxia
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoxic vasoconstriction underlies Group 3 PH from lung disease; it would be correct only with chronic hypoxemia from COPD or sleep apnea.

options.text: Chronic thromboembolic obstruction of large pulmonary arteries
options.rationale: Wrong because chronic thromboembolic disease causes Group 4 PH; it would be correct only with imaging evidence of chronic organized thrombi.

options.text: Polycythemia increasing blood viscosity and pulmonary flow resistance
options.rationale: Wrong because polycythemia can contribute to multifactorial Group 5 PH but is not the primary mechanism of PAH; it would be correct only with documented high hematocrit causing increased resistance.

question: A 32-year-old woman with progressive exertional dyspnea has right heart catheterization showing mean pulmonary arterial pressure 41 mmHg [normal 16-20] and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure 8 mmHg [normal 6-12]. According to the lecture, which vasoactive mediator is most implicated in the pathogenesis of her condition?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the pathophysiology of pulmonary hypertension

options.text: Endothelin causing vasoconstriction and smooth muscle proliferation
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture links PAH to increased endothelin-1 levels that promote vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling, especially when PAWP is normal.

options.text: Renin causing systemic vasoconstriction and volume retention
options.rationale: Wrong because renin primarily affects systemic RAAS and volume status; it would be correct only if systemic RAAS activation were the primary driver of pulmonary pressures.

options.text: Epinephrine causing transient bronchodilation and vasodilation
options.rationale: Wrong because epinephrine does not cause chronic pulmonary vascular remodeling; it would be correct only in acute sympathetic surges, not chronic PAH.

options.text: Thromboxane A2 causing platelet aggregation without vasoconstriction
options.rationale: Wrong because thromboxane contributes to platelet function and vasoconstriction but is not the central mediator emphasized in PAH pathogenesis; it would be correct only with thrombotic arteriopathy.

options.text: Nitric oxide causing vasoconstriction and smooth muscle proliferation
options.rationale: Wrong because nitric oxide is a vasodilator whose deficiency contributes to PAH; this option is incorrect in direction and would be correct only if NO were paradoxically elevated causing dysfunction.

question: Which genetic mutation discussed in the lecture is most commonly associated with familial pulmonary arterial hypertension and predisposes to endothelial dysfunction?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the pathophysiology of pulmonary hypertension

options.text: BMPR2 mutation leading to loss of antiproliferative signaling
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture identifies BMPR2 mutation as a common hereditary cause of PAH, removing inhibitory signals and promoting vascular remodeling.

options.text: CFTR mutation causing defective chloride channels in pulmonary endothelium
options.rationale: Wrong because CFTR mutations cause cystic fibrosis affecting airways, not primary PAH; it would be correct only with CF-related lung disease causing secondary PH.

options.text: Factor V Leiden causing hypercoagulability and recurrent PE
options.rationale: Wrong because Factor V Leiden predisposes to thromboembolism (Group 4 risk) but is not the classic mutation for familial PAH; it would be correct only with chronic thromboembolic disease.

options.text: HFE mutation causing iron overload and pulmonary fibrosis
options.rationale: Wrong because HFE mutations cause hemochromatosis and are not linked to primary PAH; it would be correct only if iron overload led to secondary pulmonary disease.

options.text: BRCA1 mutation causing endothelial apoptosis and vascular remodeling
options.rationale: Wrong because BRCA1 is associated with cancer risk and not PAH; it would be correct only with novel evidence linking BRCA1 to pulmonary vascular disease, which is not in the lecture.

question: A patient with systemic sclerosis develops progressive exertional dyspnea and signs of right heart strain. According to the lecture, which pulmonary vascular change best explains her pulmonary hypertension?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the pathophysiology of pulmonary hypertension

options.text: Excessive collagen deposition and intimal fibrosis in small pulmonary arterioles
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states systemic sclerosis causes connective tissue overgrowth in small pulmonary arteries, increasing resistance and producing PAH.

options.text: Alveolar destruction with loss of capillary bed as in emphysema
options.rationale: Wrong because emphysema causes vascular bed loss and Group 3 PH; it would be correct only if emphysematous destruction were the primary process.

options.text: Left atrial enlargement causing passive pulmonary venous hypertension
options.rationale: Wrong because left atrial enlargement causes Group 2 PH; it would be correct only if left-sided valvular disease or LV failure were present.

options.text: Chronic thromboembolic occlusion of segmental arteries
options.rationale: Wrong because chronic thromboembolic disease causes Group 4 PH; it would be correct only with imaging evidence of organized thrombi.

options.text: Hypoxic vasoconstriction from untreated obstructive sleep apnea
options.rationale: Wrong because hypoxic vasoconstriction is Group 3 mechanism; it would be correct only with documented chronic nocturnal hypoxemia.

question: Which hemodynamic measurement obtained by right heart catheterization, as described in the lecture, differentiates precapillary pulmonary arterial hypertension from postcapillary pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the pathophysiology of pulmonary hypertension

options.text: Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure being normal or low in precapillary disease
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that PAWP (wedge pressure) is low/normal in precapillary PAH (Group 1) and elevated in postcapillary PH from left heart disease (Group 2).

options.text: Right atrial pressure being elevated only in precapillary disease
options.rationale: Wrong because right atrial pressure can be elevated in both precapillary and postcapillary PH with RV failure; it would be correct only if RA pressure were uniquely elevated in one group.

options.text: Systemic arterial pressure being low in precapillary disease
options.rationale: Wrong because systemic arterial pressure is not the distinguishing measurement for pulmonary hypertension classification; it would be correct only with concurrent systemic hypotension.

options.text: Pulmonary artery diastolic pressure being decreased in postcapillary disease
options.rationale: Wrong because PADP is not specifically decreased in postcapillary disease; it would be correct only with unusual hemodynamics not described in the lecture.

options.text: Mixed venous oxygen saturation being elevated in precapillary disease
options.rationale: Wrong because mixed venous O₂ is not the primary discriminator between pre- and postcapillary PH; it would be correct only with specific changes in cardiac output and oxygen extraction.

question: A patient with chronic hypoxemia from COPD develops pulmonary hypertension. According to the lecture, which mechanism primarily links chronic lung disease to elevated pulmonary arterial pressure?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the pathophysiology of pulmonary hypertension

options.text: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction causing increased vascular resistance
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture identifies hypoxic vasoconstriction in chronic lung disease (Group 3 PH) as a major mechanism raising pulmonary vascular resistance and pressure.

options.text: Autoimmune-mediated endothelial proliferation identical to PAH
options.rationale: Wrong because autoimmune endothelial proliferation is characteristic of Group 1 PAH in connective tissue disease, not the primary mechanism in COPD; it would be correct only with systemic autoimmune disease.

options.text: Left ventricular diastolic dysfunction causing back pressure
options.rationale: Wrong because LV diastolic dysfunction causes Group 2 PH; it would be correct only if left heart disease were present.

options.text: Chronic thromboembolic obstruction of small arterioles
options.rationale: Wrong because chronic thromboembolic disease is Group 4 PH; it would be correct only with imaging evidence of organized thrombi.

options.text: Excessive prostacyclin production causing vasodilation and remodeling
options.rationale: Wrong because prostacyclin is vasodilatory and protective; increased prostacyclin would not cause PH and this option would be correct only if prostacyclin were paradoxically harmful, which is not in the lecture.

question: A patient with suspected pulmonary hypertension has a chest x-ray showing right ventricular enlargement and a prominent pulmonary artery knob. According to the lecture, which clinical sign on auscultation is commonly accentuated in pulmonary hypertension?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the pathophysiology of pulmonary hypertension

options.text: Accentuated second heart sound over the pulmonary valve
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes an accentuated S2 at the pulmonary valve as a common auscultatory finding in pulmonary hypertension.

options.text: Loud S3 gallop at the left lower sternal border
options.rationale: Wrong because an S3 is associated with left ventricular failure and volume overload; it would be correct only if left-sided dysfunction were present.

options.text: High-pitched holosystolic murmur at the apex
options.rationale: Wrong because an apical holosystolic murmur suggests mitral regurgitation, not primary pulmonary hypertension; it would be correct only with MR documented.

options.text: Early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation
options.rationale: Wrong because aortic regurgitation is unrelated to pulmonary hypertension; it would be correct only with valvular disease causing volume overload.

options.text: Pericardial friction rub indicating pericarditis
options.rationale: Wrong because a friction rub indicates pericardial inflammation, not pulmonary hypertension; it would be correct only with clinical pericarditis.

question: Which pharmacologic class listed in the lecture directly targets the endothelin pathway and is used to treat pulmonary arterial hypertension?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the pathophysiology of pulmonary hypertension

options.text: Endothelin receptor antagonists such as bosentan or ambrisentan
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists endothelin receptor blockers (bosentan, ambrisentan) as targeted therapy for PAH to counteract elevated endothelin-1.

options.text: ACE inhibitors such as enalapril targeting systemic RAAS
options.rationale: Wrong because ACE inhibitors primarily affect systemic RAAS and are not first-line targeted PAH therapy; they would be correct only if left heart disease were the cause of PH.

options.text: Beta blockers such as propranolol for pulmonary vasodilation
options.rationale: Wrong because beta blockers are not used to vasodilate pulmonary arteries in PAH and may be harmful; it would be correct only in specific arrhythmia management contexts.

options.text: Loop diuretics as disease-modifying agents for PAH
options.rationale: Wrong because diuretics provide symptomatic relief for volume overload but do not target endothelin-mediated remodeling; they would be correct only for symptomatic management.

options.text: Systemic corticosteroids to reverse vascular remodeling
options.rationale: Wrong because corticosteroids are not standard therapy for PAH vascular remodeling; they would be correct only in inflammatory vasculitis causing secondary PH.

question: A patient with pulmonary arterial hypertension is treated with a prostacyclin analog as described in the lecture. Which cellular effect of prostacyclin mediates its therapeutic benefit in PAH?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the pathophysiology of pulmonary hypertension

options.text: Increased cyclic AMP causing vasodilation and inhibition of smooth muscle proliferation
options.rationale: Correct because prostacyclin (PGI2) increases cAMP in vascular smooth muscle leading to vasodilation and antiproliferative effects, as outlined in the lecture's signaling slide.

options.text: Enhanced endothelin synthesis promoting vasoconstriction
options.rationale: Wrong because endothelin promotes vasoconstriction and proliferation; prostacyclin therapy would not increase endothelin and would be correct only if paradoxical endothelin upregulation occurred.

options.text: Inhibition of guanylyl cyclase reducing cGMP levels
options.rationale: Wrong because prostacyclin acts via cAMP, not by inhibiting guanylyl cyclase; this would be correct only if the drug decreased cGMP, which is not the mechanism of prostacyclin.

options.text: Blockade of L-type calcium channels preventing smooth muscle relaxation
options.rationale: Wrong because blocking L-type Ca channels reduces contraction and can cause vasodilation, but prostacyclin's primary mechanism is cAMP-mediated; this option would be correct only for calcium channel blocker therapy.

options.text: Activation of phosphodiesterase to lower intracellular cyclic nucleotides
options.rationale: Wrong because activation of PDE would reduce cAMP/cGMP and oppose vasodilation; it would be correct only if a PDE activator were used, which is not therapeutic in PAH.

question: A patient with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) is being evaluated. According to the lecture, which wedge pressure pattern and PAWP value would you expect in this form of pulmonary hypertension?
cited_learning_objective: Understand the pathophysiology of pulmonary hypertension

options.text: Precapillary pattern with pulmonary capillary wedge pressure less than 15 mmHg
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture classifies chronic thromboembolic PH (Group 4) as precapillary with PAWP  15 mmHg indicates postcapillary PH from left heart disease (Group 2), not CTEPH; it would be correct only with concomitant left-sided pathology.

options.text: Normal wedge pressure with intermittent large swings above 25 mmHg
options.rationale: Wrong because intermittent large wedge pressure swings are not characteristic of CTEPH; it would be correct only with dynamic left-sided filling abnormalities.

options.text: Wedge pressure equal to right atrial pressure indicating tamponade physiology
options.rationale: Wrong because equalization of pressures suggests tamponade, not CTEPH; it would be correct only with pericardial constriction or tamponade.

options.text: Markedly low wedge pressure below 2 mmHg from hypovolemia
options.rationale: Wrong because very low PAWP indicates hypovolemia rather than chronic thromboembolic obstruction; it would be correct only with severe volume depletion.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary edema is noted to have increased airway resistance due to peribronchiolar interstitial fluid. According to the lecture, how does this change affect ventilation-perfusion relationships and oxygenation?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the respiratory manifestations of pulmonary edema

options.text: Narrowed bronchioles reduce ventilation causing low V/Q units and hypoxemia
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that peribronchiolar edema narrows airways, decreasing ventilation relative to perfusion (low V/Q) and contributing to hypoxemia.

options.text: Increased airway resistance causes uniform dead space ventilation improving oxygenation
options.rationale: Wrong because increased resistance does not create dead space that improves oxygenation; it would be correct only if ventilation increased relative to perfusion, which is not the case.

options.text: Airway narrowing increases diffusion capacity and raises PaO₂
options.rationale: Wrong because diffusion capacity is reduced with edema and airway narrowing worsens oxygenation; it would be correct only with paradoxical physiologic changes not described in the lecture.

options.text: Bronchiolar narrowing causes hyperventilation of affected units lowering PaO₂
options.rationale: Wrong because affected units are hypoventilated, not hyperventilated; this would be correct only if ventilation increased selectively to diseased units.

options.text: Peribronchiolar edema increases alveolar recruitment and improves V/Q matching
options.rationale: Wrong because edema reduces alveolar recruitment and worsens V/Q matching; it would be correct only with therapeutic interventions like PEEP improving recruitment.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary edema is placed on supplemental oxygen. According to the lecture, why is supplemental oxygen recommended in pulmonary edema?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the respiratory manifestations of pulmonary edema

options.text: To increase alveolar oxygen partial pressure and reduce hypoxemia from shunt and low V/Q
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture recommends supplemental oxygen since flooded alveoli cause shunt and low V/Q, and increasing inspired O₂ helps raise PaO₂ in ventilated units.

options.text: To decrease pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure directly
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen does not directly lower hydrostatic pressure; it would be correct only if oxygen indirectly improved cardiac output and reduced backpressure.

options.text: To resolve alveolar fluid by increasing lymphatic drainage
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen does not clear alveolar fluid; it would be correct only with interventions that enhance lymphatic flow or diuresis.

options.text: To treat the underlying cardiac cause of pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen is supportive therapy and does not treat the cardiac etiology; it would be correct only if oxygen improved myocardial ischemia indirectly.

options.text: To reduce capillary permeability in noncardiogenic edema
options.rationale: Wrong because oxygen does not reduce capillary permeability; it would be correct only if anti-inflammatory therapy addressed permeability.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary embolism has a complete obstruction of a segmental pulmonary artery. According to the lecture, what is the most likely immediate effect on the A-a gradient for oxygen?
cited_learning_objective: Understand clinical manifestations of pulmonary embolism

options.text: A widened alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient due to increased dead space and V/Q mismatch
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that PE increases dead space and redistributes perfusion causing V/Q mismatch and an increased A-a gradient leading to hypoxemia.

options.text: A narrowed A-a gradient reflecting improved oxygenation
options.rationale: Wrong because PE worsens oxygenation and widens the A-a gradient; it would be correct only with improved ventilation or resolution of obstruction.

options.text: No change in A-a gradient because PaO₂ and PAO₂ change equally
options.rationale: Wrong because PE causes disproportionate arterial hypoxemia relative to alveolar oxygen, widening the gradient; it would be correct only in rare balanced changes.

options.text: A decreased A-a gradient due to hyperventilation lowering PaCO₂
options.rationale: Wrong because hyperventilation lowers PaCO₂ but does not decrease the A-a gradient caused by perfusion defects; it would be correct only if alveolar oxygen rose more than arterial oxygen.

options.text: A variable A-a gradient that becomes normal with supplemental oxygen
options.rationale: Wrong because supplemental oxygen may raise PaO₂ but does not normalize the underlying widened A-a gradient from V/Q mismatch; it would be correct only if oxygen corrected the mismatch fully.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary edema is noted to have jugular venous pressure of 10 cm H₂O. According to the lecture, which interpretation of this JVP value is most consistent with impaired cardiac filling?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the respiratory manifestations of pulmonary edema

options.text: Elevated JVP suggesting increased central venous pressure and impaired cardiac filling
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture indicates that elevated JVP reflects increased central venous pressure often seen with heart failure and impaired cardiac filling contributing to hydrostatic pulmonary edema.

options.text: Low JVP indicating hypovolemia as the cause of pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Wrong because low JVP suggests hypovolemia, which does not cause hydrostatic pulmonary edema; it would be correct only if the patient were volume depleted.

options.text: Normal JVP excluding cardiac causes of pulmonary edema
options.rationale: Wrong because normal JVP does not exclude cardiac causes; it would be correct only if other signs and wedge pressure were normal.

options.text: Fluctuating JVP indicating primary pulmonary vasculitis
options.rationale: Wrong because fluctuating JVP is not diagnostic of pulmonary vasculitis; it would be correct only with additional inflammatory and imaging evidence.

options.text: Elevated JVP due to isolated tricuspid regurgitation without left heart involvement
options.rationale: Wrong because isolated TR raises JVP but does not directly explain pulmonary edema from left-sided hydrostatic pressure; it would be correct only if TR were the primary pathology.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary edema secondary to left ventricular infarction is hypertensive. According to the lecture, which adjunctive therapy may be used to reduce afterload and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure in this setting?
cited_learning_objective: Compare pathophysiological manifestations of cardiogenic and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema

options.text: Vasodilator therapy to lower systemic vascular resistance and reduce pulmonary venous pressure
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists vasodilators for hypertensive cardiogenic pulmonary edema to decrease afterload and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure.

options.text: High-dose intravenous corticosteroids to reduce capillary permeability
options.rationale: Wrong because corticosteroids target permeability in inflammatory edema, not hydrostatic pressure; it would be correct only in noncardiogenic inflammatory edema like FES.

options.text: Aggressive fluid bolus to increase preload and cardiac output
options.rationale: Wrong because fluid bolus worsens hydrostatic pulmonary edema from LV failure; it would be correct only if the patient were hypovolemic with low filling pressures.

options.text: Inhaled bronchodilators to reduce pulmonary vascular resistance
options.rationale: Wrong because bronchodilators act on airways and do not significantly reduce pulmonary venous pressure; it would be correct only if bronchospasm were a major contributor.

options.text: Immediate initiation of systemic thrombolysis
options.rationale: Wrong because thrombolysis treats thromboembolic obstruction, not cardiogenic edema from LV infarction; it would be correct only if PE were the cause.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary edema is noted to have interstitial edema with perivascular cuffing but relatively preserved pulmonary function. According to the lecture, which stage of edema does this description represent and why is gas exchange relatively preserved?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the respiratory manifestations of pulmonary edema

options.text: Interstitial edema stage where lymphatic flow increases and alveoli remain largely air-filled
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture describes interstitial edema as early stage with perivascular cuffing and increased lymph flow; pulmonary function is minimally affected until alveolar flooding occurs.

options.text: Alveolar edema stage where surfactant is diluted causing severe hypoxemia
options.rationale: Wrong because alveolar edema causes marked gas exchange impairment; this would be correct only if alveoli were filled with fluid and shunting occurred.

options.text: Chronic fibrotic stage with irreversible interstitial scarring
options.rationale: Wrong because chronic fibrosis is a late, long-term change not the acute interstitial edema stage; it would be correct only with chronic disease and imaging showing fibrosis.

options.text: Pleural effusion stage where fluid compresses lung bases causing restrictive physiology
options.rationale: Wrong because pleural effusion is distinct from interstitial edema and causes compression rather than perivascular cuffing; it would be correct only with large pleural fluid on imaging.

options.text: Pulmonary hemorrhage stage with alveolar blood filling causing hemoptysis
options.rationale: Wrong because pulmonary hemorrhage produces bloody alveolar filling and severe dysfunction; it would be correct only with evidence of bleeding into alveoli.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary edema demonstrates rapid shallow breathing as an adaptive response. According to the lecture, why does rapid shallow breathing minimize the elastic work of breathing in this setting?
cited_learning_objective: Analyze the respiratory manifestations of pulmonary edema

options.text: Smaller tidal volumes reduce the elastic recoil work required to expand stiff, less-compliant lungs
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture explains that decreased compliance from edema makes deep breaths costly; rapid shallow breathing reduces elastic work by using smaller tidal volumes.

options.text: Rapid shallow breaths increase alveolar recruitment and improve compliance
options.rationale: Wrong because shallow breaths do not recruit alveoli effectively; recruitment typically requires larger tidal volumes or PEEP and this option would be correct only with those interventions.

options.text: Shallow breathing increases diaphragmatic efficiency by lengthening muscle fibers
options.rationale: Wrong because diaphragmatic mechanics are not improved by shallow breathing in edema; it would be correct only with specific neuromuscular adaptations.

options.text: Rapid shallow breathing reduces airway resistance by increasing laminar flow
options.rationale: Wrong because increased respiratory rate often raises airway resistance and work; this would be correct only in specific flow dynamics not typical in edema.

options.text: Shallow breaths lower metabolic CO₂ production reducing ventilatory demand
options.rationale: Wrong because tidal volume changes do not significantly alter metabolic CO₂ production; it would be correct only with major metabolic suppression.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary edema secondary to fluid overload is treated with intravenous furosemide. According to the lecture, which immediate physiologic effect of loop diuretics helps reduce pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure?
cited_learning_objective: Compare pathophysiological manifestations of cardiogenic and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema

options.text: Reduction of intravascular volume decreasing venous return and pulmonary venous pressure
options.rationale: Correct because loop diuretics reduce circulating volume, lowering venous return and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, which decreases transudation into alveoli as taught in the lecture.

options.text: Direct increase of alveolar fluid clearance by stimulating lymphatics
options.rationale: Wrong because diuretics do not directly stimulate lymphatic clearance; this would be correct only if a drug specifically enhanced lymphatic flow.

options.text: Immediate restoration of surfactant concentration in flooded alveoli
options.rationale: Wrong because diuretics do not restore surfactant; surfactant dilution is corrected by removing fluid over time or with specific therapies.

options.text: Direct blockade of pulmonary capillary permeability to prevent leakage
options.rationale: Wrong because loop diuretics do not alter capillary permeability; this would be correct only with anti-inflammatory agents that reduce permeability.

options.text: Vasoconstriction of pulmonary arterioles to divert blood away from edematous regions
options.rationale: Wrong because diuretics do not cause pulmonary vasoconstriction; it would be correct only with agents that induce pulmonary vasoconstriction, which are not therapeutic in edema.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary embolism has a ventilation-perfusion scan showing multiple segmental perfusion defects with preserved ventilation. According to the lecture, which clinical sign is most likely to be present if pulmonary infarction has occurred?
cited_learning_objective: Understand clinical manifestations of pulmonary embolism

options.text: Pleuritic chest pain and hemoptysis from peripheral infarction
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes that peripheral emboli near the pleura can cause pleuritic pain and hemoptysis when infarction occurs.

options.text: Diffuse wheezing without chest pain
options.rationale: Wrong because diffuse wheezing is more typical of bronchospasm; it would be correct only with coexisting reactive airway disease.

options.text: High fever and productive purulent sputum
options.rationale: Wrong because fever and purulent sputum suggest infection rather than infarction; it would be correct only with secondary infection.

options.text: Isolated syncope without respiratory symptoms
options.rationale: Wrong because syncope can occur in massive PE but isolated syncope without respiratory signs is less typical of infarction; it would be correct only in massive central PE.

options.text: Gradual onset exertional dyspnea over months
options.rationale: Wrong because infarction causes acute symptoms; gradual exertional dyspnea suggests chronic cardiopulmonary disease and would be correct only with chronic pathology.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary embolism is hemodynamically stable but has a high clinical probability. According to the lecture, which initial management step is most appropriate while diagnostic imaging is arranged?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the diagnostic options for pulmonary embolism

options.text: Begin anticoagulation with heparin unless contraindicated
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture emphasizes anticoagulation (eg, heparin) as primary management for suspected PE and prevention, started promptly when not contraindicated while imaging is pending.

options.text: Administer systemic thrombolytics immediately in all suspected cases
options.rationale: Wrong because thrombolytics are reserved for massive PE with hemodynamic compromise; they would be correct only if the patient were unstable or in shock.

options.text: Place an inferior vena cava filter before anticoagulation
options.rationale: Wrong because IVC filters are for selected patients with contraindications to anticoagulation or recurrent PE; it would be correct only if anticoagulation were contraindicated.

options.text: Withhold anticoagulation and observe until V/Q scan confirms diagnosis
options.rationale: Wrong because delaying anticoagulation in high-probability PE risks propagation; it would be correct only if bleeding risk were prohibitive.

options.text: Start high-dose corticosteroids to reduce pulmonary inflammation
options.rationale: Wrong because corticosteroids are not indicated for thromboembolic PE; they would be correct only in inflammatory causes like FES or ARDS.

question: A patient with acute pulmonary edema has bilateral diffuse infiltrates on chest x-ray but no cardiomegaly and a normal PCWP. According to the lecture, which ventilatory strategy is recommended for severe noncardiogenic pulmonary edema?
cited_learning_objective: Compare pathophysiological manifestations of cardiogenic and non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema

options.text: Mechanical ventilation with positive end-expiratory pressure to improve oxygenation
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture recommends mechanical ventilation with PEEP for noncardiogenic edema (eg, ARDS) to recruit alveoli and improve oxygenation.

options.text: High tidal volume ventilation without PEEP to maximize minute ventilation
options.rationale: Wrong because high tidal volumes can worsen lung injury; lung-protective strategies with PEEP are preferred and this would be correct only in rare circumstances.

options.text: Immediate diuretics as first-line therapy
options.rationale: Wrong because diuretics are not recommended for noncardiogenic edema unless volume overload is present; it would be correct only with concurrent fluid overload.

options.text: Inhaled nitric oxide as sole therapy to remove alveolar fluid
options.rationale: Wrong because inhaled NO may transiently improve V/Q matching but does not remove alveolar fluid; it would be correct only as adjunctive therapy in select cases.

options.text: Prone positioning without ventilatory support
options.rationale: Wrong because prone positioning is an adjunct to mechanical ventilation in ARDS, not a replacement for ventilatory support; it would be correct only when combined with ventilation.

question: A patient with suspected pulmonary embolism cannot undergo CTPA due to severe renal impairment. According to the lecture, which diagnostic test is the preferred alternative to evaluate for PE in this situation?
cited_learning_objective: Outline the diagnostic options for pulmonary embolism

options.text: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan to assess mismatched perfusion defects
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture states V/Q scanning is reserved when CTPA is contraindicated (eg, renal failure or contrast allergy) and can detect perfusion defects relative to ventilation.

options.text: Pulmonary angiography as the routine noncontrast alternative
options.rationale: Wrong because invasive pulmonary angiography is not the routine alternative and carries procedural risk; it would be correct only if noninvasive tests were inconclusive and intervention planned.

options.text: Lower extremity venography to directly visualize pulmonary arteries
options.rationale: Wrong because lower extremity venography images leg veins, not pulmonary arteries; it would be correct only if DVT were found and PE imaging contraindicated.

options.text: Transthoracic echocardiography to definitively exclude PE
options.rationale: Wrong because echocardiography can suggest RV strain but cannot definitively exclude PE; it would be correct only as a bedside tool in unstable patients.

options.text: Chest radiograph alone to rule out pulmonary embolism
options.rationale: Wrong because chest x-ray lacks sensitivity and specificity for PE; it would be correct only as an initial screening but not definitive.
